title: OrchestrateDASH agent manifest v2
description: Additive v2 manifest. It preserves the telemetry v1 fields and adds an Agent DOM declaration. Unknown fields remain forward-compatible. Credential values are forbidden; connection fields describe requirements only.

expected_interval_seconds.description: The longest gap DASH should expect between this agent's activity before treating it as stalled rather than quietly idle. Optional and meaningful only alongside type "schedule": schedule is free text ("weekdays at 08:00 local time") and DASH does not parse it, so an absent value means no expectation can be derived and this agent is never marked stalled.

task_inputs.description: What files this agent accepts as a task, declared per role (MAR-434). Optional, and absent means the agent takes no files — which is every agent shipped before this block existed, so absence must never be read as an unrestricted agent. The declaration is what the runner narrows its own ceilings down to; it can never widen them, so a manifest asking for a 4 GiB input gets the runner's limit and a refusal, not 4 GiB. See runner/workspace.ts effectiveLimits.

taskInputRole.description:
One kind of file a task accepts, in the user's vocabulary (MAR-434).

A role rather than a slot number, because the surface says "Customer brief" and "Price list" and a person selects against those words. `id` is what a command carries and never what a person reads — the split `permissionGrant` already makes, for the same reason.

**Media types are checked against sniffed bytes, not against the extension.** An extension is a claim by whoever named the file; `runner/workspace.ts` reads the first bytes and refuses a mismatch. So declaring `application/pdf` here means the runner will refuse a renamed executable, and declaring nothing means the runner does not narrow — which is honest but is not the same as accepting anything, because the runner's own ceilings still apply.

id.description: Technical vocabulary, e.g. `customer_brief`. Carried in commands; never rendered on a guided surface.

label.description: What a person reads, e.g. "Customer brief". Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

description.description: Why this agent wants it. Rendered beside the file picker so a person can tell whether they are handing over the right document.

required.description: Whether the task can start without it. Required rather than optional in the schema because a renderer that has to guess would guess `false` and let a task start missing the file it exists to read.

max_count.description: The runner lowers this to its own ceiling and never raises it.

media_types.description: Accepted types as the runner sniffs them, e.g. `application/pdf`. Absent means the runner does not narrow by type. Note that DASH does not open a ZIP container to tell a .docx from a .xlsx, so both are `application/zip` — declaring one and not the other narrows nothing.

max_file_bytes.description: Per file. Lowered to the runner's ceiling, never raised past it.

max_total_bytes.description: Across every file in this role. Lowered to the runner's ceiling, never raised past it.

panel.description:
The agent's own panel, declared rather than programmed (ADR 0008, MAR-552).

A panel is **data over a closed vocabulary** that DASH renders with its own trusted components. Agent-authored code never executes in DASH's renderer, and this block is not an escape hatch from that: what a panel can make DASH draw is one closed union, readable in `$defs.panelSectionV1` in a single sitting.

The absences are the argument. **No component takes a URL. No component takes markup. No component takes a path. No component takes an image. No component names another agent. No component asks the user for anything, and no event vocabulary exists.** Widening any of those means widening a pinned union in a reviewed commit, which is the by-value-pin discipline doing its job.

Optional, and **omitted when undeclared — never an empty object**, the exact rule `task_inputs` shipped with. Absence means the author declared no panel; it must never be read as "render something anyway".

panel_version.description: Which vocabulary the sections are written in. Version 1 is the closed five-component set below. See the if/then/else: a version DASH knows is checked strictly, a version it does not know is accepted structurally and rendered as one stated card.

title.description: What the author calls this panel. Rendered as a text node inside a region DASH itself heads, so it reads as the author's words and cannot be mistaken for a DASH verdict. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

sections.description: In render order. Bounded here rather than defended against in the renderer: a spec that cannot describe an unbounded render is better than a renderer that has to survive one.

panelSectionV1.description:
One section of a version 1 panel. The `type` enum is closed on purpose: a typo'd type is refused at import, loudly, rather than silently dropped at render — a half-drawn panel is a guess rendered as a fact.

Each branch of the oneOf below is discriminated by `type`, so a section matches exactly one shape and the renderer can narrow on the same field the author wrote.

id.description: Technical vocabulary, e.g. `latest_digest`. Travels so a section can be addressed; never rendered, the same split `taskInputRole.id` and `permissionGrant.id` already make.

label.description: What a person reads at the head of the section. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

type.description: The closed vocabulary, complete in this one array. `report` is the newest artifact of a role; `outputs` is the artifact cards filtered by role; `table` is rows from the newest JSON artifact of a role; `metrics` is labelled values from an artifact field or from a fact DASH itself observes; `note` is a bounded block of the author's own copy.

oneOf.description: report — the newest artifact of the named role, rendered through the artifact-card and digest machinery the run detail page already uses, receipt included.
outputs — the existing Outputs area, placeable and scopeable by the author. An absent `artifact_role` means every role this agent produced, which is what the Outputs area already shows.

table — rows from the newest JSON artifact of `source_role` whose body is an array of objects. A cell is an own-property lookup by `key`, rendered per `kind`; a value that is not the declared kind renders as absent, never coerced. There is deliberately no path or expression syntax: a path language is an interpreter, and interpreters grow.

key.description: One own property of a row object. An alphabet that cannot spell a separator, a traversal or a URL.

kind.description: How the cell is rendered. A value of a different kind renders as absent rather than being coerced, because a coerced cell is DASH asserting something the agent did not say.

oneOf.description: metrics — labelled values from either a top-level field of a JSON artifact or from the closed set of facts DASH itself observes. The two sources render differently attributed: an artifact field is *the agent's report*, a dash fact is *DASH's record*. Collapsing that distinction would let an agent's own number wear DASH's voice — it is `stated_at`/`received_at`'s split, applied to a number.
The agent's own report: one top-level field of the newest JSON artifact of this role.
DASH's own record. A closed set, each member already computed for an existing view — nothing here asks DASH to derive something new on an agent's behalf.

note — a bounded block of author copy, with the same standing as the manifest's `goal`: the author's words, rendered as the author's words, inside a region DASH heads as the author's own panel. An author can still be wrong in a note; the mitigation is attribution, not censorship, and DASH's verdict surfaces render outside the panel where no section can imitate them.

panelSectionOpaque.description:
A section of a panel version DASH does not know (ADR 0008).

Checked for structure only, so the document is accepted rather than rejected — the contract's additive-versioning rule, which lib/contracts.ts states as "DASH ignores what it does not understand rather than rejecting the document". DASH renders such a panel as **one stated card** saying the author declared it in a newer format, never section by section: a partially drawn panel is a guess presented as a fact.

`type` is an open string here precisely because the closed enum belongs to version 1 and must not rot into leniency to accommodate a version that has not been designed yet.

connectionRequirements.description:
What this agent needs connected, and which flow DASH launches to connect it (MAR-569).

**Read the name carefully: this is not `$defs.connectionRequirement`.** That one is the per-credential inventory behind `agent_dom.connections` — who holds the secret, which fields exist, how a test is run. This block is the shorter, DASH-first question a person actually arrives with: *what still needs connecting, and what happens when I press the button?* The two describe the same connections from opposite ends, and a v1 requirement names its `connection_id` so DASH can check that they agree rather than trusting that they do.

The standing correction ADR 0008 makes about panels holds here word for word: **what travels is a declaration, not code.** The agent says what it needs; DASH's own trusted flows do the connecting. `connector_kind` is a closed enum of flows DASH has actually built, because a kind DASH cannot launch is a lie on a button.

Optional, and **omitted when undeclared — never an empty object**, the rule `task_inputs` and `panel` both shipped with. Absence means the author declared nothing here; it must never be read as "this agent needs nothing connected" — `agent_dom.connections` is still the inventory, and every agent built before this block existed has one.

requirements_version.description: Which vocabulary the requirements are written in. Version 1 is the closed two-flow set below. See the if/then/else: a version DASH knows is checked strictly, a version it does not know is accepted structurally and drawn as one stated card. A new connector kind arrives by bumping this, never by widening version 1's enum in place.

requirements.description: In the order a person should work through them. Bounded here rather than defended against in the surface, the same argument `panel.sections` makes: a spec that cannot describe an unbounded list is better than a page that has to survive one.

connectionRequirementV1.description:
One thing that needs connecting, in a version 1 declaration (MAR-569).

`connector_kind` is closed on purpose and a typo'd kind is refused at import, loudly, rather than dropped at render — the same refusal `$defs.panelSectionV1` makes, for the same reason. The failure it prevents is worse here than on a panel: a requirement DASH cannot place is a line on the Connections page with a Connect button that fires nothing, which teaches a person that DASH's buttons are decorative.

Every member below is either plain language a person reads or an identifier DASH resolves against something it already holds. **Nothing here is a URL, a path, a host, or a credential**, and the `propertyNames` guard repeats the manifest-wide rule that a connection block describes requirements and never carries a value.

id.description: Technical vocabulary, so a requirement can be addressed by the surface and the emitter. Travels; never rendered — `lib/copy/identifiers.ts`'s rule.

name.description: What the user sees on the line: "Your Gmail", "A Notion workspace". Plain language, the author's words, and the only member of this object a person reads. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts, which is what stops it being a provider slug in disguise.

connector_kind.description:
Which flow DASH launches. Closed to the two DASH has actually built: `google_oauth_broker` is MAR-458's brokered sign-in, `api_key` is DASH-custodied secret entry through the credential prompt.

**Two, not three, and the missing one is the point.** MAR-569 as filed named a third kind, `mcp_server`, attributed to MAR-498's wizard. That wizard connects an SSH deploy host — an address, a username, a key name, a pinned fingerprint — so an agent can be *put on a server*. It cannot connect a Notion workspace, and DASH has no MCP-server connect flow anywhere: `remote_mcp_server` exists only as a `TokenCustodian` label whose own docblock records that `dash_vault` is the sole reachable value. Shipping the kind would have produced exactly what this enum exists to prevent, and Henrik's ruling on 2026-08-08 was to drop it.

A real MCP-server flow arrives the way any fourth kind does: a version bump, structurally accepted by the `else` branch above and drawn as one stated "DASH cannot connect this yet" line — never a dead Connect button. Widening this enum in place is widening what a manifest can make DASH offer to do, which is why it is a by-value pin in a reviewed commit.

connection_id.description:
Which entry of `agent_dom.connections` this requirement is about, by its `id`. Required, because both v1 kinds act on a declared connection.

That is not bookkeeping: it is what makes the requirement checkable. DASH resolves the standing of each named operation through the existing three-party intersection on that connection, and the Connect button acts on that connection's field. A requirement that named no connection could only be drawn as a sentence with a dead button beside it — and an id naming a connection this manifest never declared is a disagreement between two of its own blocks, which DASH surfaces rather than repairs.

operations.description:
The operations this requirement needs, by the id `lib/broker/operations.ts` gives them.

These feed the requested-vs-unrequested intersection the capability cards already draw, so a requirement resolves to the same four standings a capability does. Absent means the requirement names no operations of its own and DASH reads the whole connection's requested set — the honest default, since `agent_dom.connections` already declared the scopes.

An operation named here that the connection never declared is a **disagreement between two blocks of one manifest**, and DASH surfaces it rather than rounding it into "not connected": the fix is a re-export, not a sign-in.

optional.description:
Whether this agent can run without it. Absent means required.

The reading that matters is the false one: an agent that can run degraded says so here, and one that cannot stays silent. A surface may then tell the truth a checklist could not — that three of these four are what the agent actually needs, and the fourth adds something.

why.description: What the agent does with it, in the author's words and with the same standing as the manifest's `goal` — the author's claim, rendered as the author's claim. Optional, because an author with nothing to add should say nothing rather than pad the line.

connectionRequirementOpaque.description:
A requirement from a declaration version DASH does not know (MAR-569).

Checked for structure only, so the document is accepted rather than rejected — the contract's additive-versioning rule. DASH draws such a declaration as **one stated card** saying the author declared it in a newer format, never line by line with buttons: a Connect button DASH resolved by guessing is worse than no button, and it is the same argument `$defs.panelSectionOpaque` makes about a half-drawn panel.

`connector_kind` is an open string here precisely because the closed enum belongs to version 1 and must not rot into leniency to accommodate a version that has not been designed yet.

roleName.description: An artifact role, e.g. `digest`. Bindings name roles and never locations — MAR-507's rule ("the renderer names a kind of file and never a file") applied to data binding. The alphabet cannot spell a separator, a traversal or a URL, and the binding carries no agent, so a panel resolves roles against *this* agent's runs and cannot reach another's.

permissions.description:
What the agent declares it may do that needs no credential — the case `connections` cannot express, because every connection requirement carries an owner, fields and a validation action. Additive and optional: a manifest without this block declares nothing, which is different from declaring nothing is needed.

The shape deliberately mirrors the OrchestrateKit registry's component `permissions` block (read / write / approval_required_for) so a scaffolded manifest and an exported build brief describe a permission the same way. A second vocabulary here would mean the two documents could disagree about the same grant.

**This is a declaration, not a boundary.** The runner strips the environment (`runner/supervisor.ts`) but spawns an ordinary child process with unrestricted network access. DASH renders what the agent claims and who to ask about it; it does not enforce it, and no copy built on this block may say that it does. The same honesty ADR 0002 requires of the draft-only Gmail boundary applies here.

browser.description:
The browser this agent asks DASH to open for it (MAR-628, ADR 0019). Additive and optional: a manifest without this block asks for no browser, which is every agent shipped before it existed.

**Unlike `permissions`, this one is enforced** — and only for the browser DASH provides. DASH opens an ephemeral Chromium view inside its own window, checks every request that view makes against `origins`, and refuses the rest. It does not and cannot constrain the agent's own process, which has an ordinary network stack; `lib/browser/origins.ts` carries the sentence every surface must use, and no copy built on this block may say an agent could only reach these addresses.

The block is separate from `permissions` precisely because that one's contract is "DASH does not enforce this". An enforced list inside the unenforced block would have made both halves unreadable.

What DASH decides and the author does not is the **operation catalogue**: an agent may open a page and read the words on it, and nothing else. There is no click, no typing, no scrolling, no second tab and no arbitrary JavaScript, because `lib/browser/operations.ts` contains no such operation — see ADR 0019 amendment 1 for what slice 1 shipped and what stays deferred.

purpose.description: Why this agent needs a browser, in the words a person reads before they run it. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts: plain language, no operation ids, no addresses.

origins.description:
Exact HTTPS origins, and exactly that — a scheme, a host and an optional port, with no path, no query and no fragment. `https://example.com/news` is refused rather than accepted-and-widened, because an origin has no path and silently granting the whole host while the manifest, the card and the person all read a directory is the failure ADR 0019 names first. A prefix match is not used anywhere: `https://example.com.attacker.test` is not inside `https://example.com`.

List every origin the page actually needs, including the ones it does not choose — scripts, fonts, images and API calls are requests the controlled browser makes and are held to this same list. An article whose stylesheet lives on a CDN needs the CDN named here or the page renders without it.

id.description: The registry's own name for the capability, e.g. `network`. Technical vocabulary: a guided surface renders `label`, never this.

label.description: What it may do, in the words a person reads. Held to lib/copy/identifiers.ts.

detail.description: The scope of the grant in plain language — what is included and what is not.

connectionRequirement.description:
One connection this agent declares, as an inventory entry: who holds the credential, which fields it has, and how a test is run against it. This is what `agent_dom.connections` is made of, and it is the source the permission cards and the vault both read.

**Not to be confused with `$defs.connectionRequirements` (plural)**, added by MAR-569, which is the shorter DASH-first declaration of *what still needs connecting and which flow connects it*. A v1 entry there names one of these by `id`. Same connections, opposite ends: this one is the record, that one is the next action.

access.description: `spend` since MAR-619, and it is a correction rather than a new idea: BrokerAccess has had three members since MAR-545 and lib/connections.ts's RequiredCapability has typed this field as all three ever since, so this schema was the last place still saying there were two — and an author declaring a capability that costs money had no honest word for it. It means what it means there: the person's own account is charged and nothing appears anywhere. Filing such a capability under `write` would make a card claim something turns up in an account, which is the one thing a completion does not do.
access.$comment: Additive: no existing manifest declares it, and every reader already narrows on the wider union.
